lesson.title: Dynamic Range: From Whisper to Shout Without Breaking
lesson.summary: Dynamic range is the decibel span between a system's noise floor and the loudest signal it can pass without distorting, describing how wide a range of levels, quiet to loud, the system can handle cleanly all at once.
lesson.body:
Signal-to-noise ratio, from the previous chapter, compares one particular signal level to the noise floor. Dynamic range asks a related but distinct question: instead of looking at just one signal level, it compares the maximum signal the system can pass cleanly to the noise floor at the bottom. In other words, SNR tells you how clean one specific signal is, while dynamic range tells you how wide a span, from the quietest recoverable detail up to the loudest signal before things go wrong, the system can capture at once, without needing to be readjusted in between.

The formula has the same shape as SNR: Dynamic Range (dB) = 20 times log10(V max divided by V noise), where V max is the largest voltage the system can produce or pass through without the signal starting to distort. Exactly what happens once a signal tries to exceed that ceiling is formalized later in this sequence, under the name clipping; for now, just treat V max as the largest clean output voltage the circuit is capable of.

Here is a worked example, reusing the same noise floor as before. Suppose the noise floor is 2 mV RMS (0.002 V), and the largest clean output this system can produce is 10 V RMS. Dynamic range = 20 times log10(10 divided by 0.002). The ratio is 10 divided by 0.002, which equals 5000. The base ten log of 5000 equals log10(5) plus log10(1000), which is 0.699 plus 3, giving 3.699. Multiplying by 20 gives 73.98, so the dynamic range here is about 74.0 dB.

A system with wide dynamic range can capture a whispered passage and a loud crescendo in the same take without the quiet part sinking into the noise floor or the loud part overshooting the system's ceiling. Digital audio ties directly into this idea: each additional bit of resolution in a digital system adds roughly 6 dB of usable dynamic range, which is why 16 bit digital audio is commonly cited as having a theoretical dynamic range of roughly 96 dB. Headroom, covered next, looks specifically at the upper portion of this same range, the gap between where a signal normally sits and where that ceiling actually is.
